catalog_quote: 2. Tone and Stress 2a. There appear to be three main tone levels in these languages—High, Mid, and Low. Rising and Falling tones are common ... 2b. Stress is often responsible for changes in vowel quality and vowel length. In MAYOGO there is a tendency towards vowel length on the penultimate syllable. In NGBAKA, GBAYA, and BANDA, on the other hand, there is a tendency towards extra shortness here. Compare Eboué’s BANDA spellings yavro (dog), yabru (goat), akblo (child) with Hackett’s TOGBO renderings yavor6 [scan; = yavoró], aboro, agbolo. 3. Word Shape The simplest form of the word is monosyllabic: CV (but VCV in some languages). [Section 1 of the same chapter, after the MAYOGO items éngu/ongu: ‘Long vowels and diphthongs are absent. Nasalized vowels are common in BANDA, GBAYA, and NGBANDI, absent ...’]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mayogo is a three-level tone language (H, M, L); under 'Stress' the handbook reports only a tendency for the penultimate syllable to carry vowel length, i.e. penultimate prominence realized as lengthening (Tucker's own Mayogo-of-Niangara field data). No explicit rule of stress placement, no claim that stress is contrastive.
new_statements.exceptions: Stated only as a 'tendency'; contrasted with Ngbaka, Gbaya and Banda, where the penultimate vowel tends instead to be extra short/elided.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level remark in a comparative handbook chapter covering the whole Sere-Mundu and Banda-Gbaya-Ngbandi group; based on isolated citation forms in Tucker's field notes. It is an indirect stress statement (length as the correlate) and should be superseded by Sawka 2001 / McCord 1989 if they treat stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's Mayogo data are Tucker's own notes on 'MAYOGO (of Niangara)' (Haut-Uele, DR Congo) = Mayogo proper, glottocode mayo1261; no dialect named (Ethnologue dialects: Madimadoko, Madipia). The statement sits in a group chapter (Sere-Mundu + Banda-Gbaya-Ngbandi) but the quoted sentence is explicitly about Mayogo.
